newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Investors jittery over threat to sack Kazakh PM.
newsitem.headline: Investors jittery over threat to sack Kazakh PM.

text.p: Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev's threat to sack his reformist prime minister sent jitters through the foreign investment community in the resource-rich former Soviet republic on Tuesday.

With his popularity waning as fast as the backlog of unpaid wages and pensions grows, Nazarbayev late on Monday sought in Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin a handy political scapegoat for Kazakhstan's payments crisis.
"I give April 10 as the deadline and he (Kazhegeldin) should by then tell how he will resolve this problem -- or leave," he lashed out at a meeting of government and regional officials.
Few Kazakhs or western investors like to venture political comment in the republic where Nazarbayev, the country's Soviet-era Communist Party boss, keeps a tight rein on power.
But according to one western financier in the capital Almaty, "Kazhegeldin can't pay off 30 billion tenge ($400 million) in wage arrears in a month -- it would be a disaster for the economy."
The financier added: "With Kazhegeldin comes a whole host of other reform-minded officials at the National Bank and other institutions -- his departure would be a disaster."
Another western investor said the president's move against Kazhegeldin showed Nazarbeyev "out of touch with what's going on in the economy."

Kazhegeldin, 45, a businessman before his appointment in 1994, won praise from western institutions for slashing inflation to around 30 percent in 1996, building the republic's financial structures and an ambitious privatisation programme.
But his government has done little to address the widespread political resentment caused by the hardships faced by many of his compatriots.

The only change much of the 16.9 million population scattered across this country of bleak steppe land have felt since independence in 1991 is a widening hole in their pockets and frozen homes from a lack of electricity and gas.
"Kazhegeldin's government has had three years in power without positive results," said an independent deputy in the Kazakh parliament, Engels Gabbasov.
"He took the example of developed countries but a securities market and other innovations don't work here," Gabbasov told Reuters. "Nazarbayev was forced to make changes in the government," he said.

Observers say even if Kazhegeldin is permitted to stay on past the April deadline, a new power structure emerging from a slew of new appointments published in the official press this week leaves the prime minister with substantially less power.

Most important is Nurlan Balgimbayev's move from heading the oil and gas ministry to lead a new state-owned concern, Kazakh Oil, where he will report direct to Nazarbayev and no longer to Kazhegeldin.
Balgimbayev has fought tooth and nail against Kazhegeldin's planned fire-sale of state-owned oil enterprises to foreign investors with the necessary cash to revive the ailing industry.
Balgimbayev and the enterprises' Soviet-era "red directors" do not want the industry -- worth billions of dollars -- to fall under foreign management or control.
Kazakh Oil will now hold 40-50 percent stakes in all energy ventures which would appear to mark a major defeat for Kazhelgeldin in his struggle with the country's oil barons.
However, one western investor took a sanguine view.
"I don't think the market will be affected that much," he said. "I think what will change will be the players in that market," he said.
